question: When machines were promised to replace translators and interpreters, what actually happened to the people who carry words between languages, and which part of the work stays with people?

issues.note: Cut from the library reading room to an empty, dark Nuremberg courtroom. The narration 'a few years later: a trial' is the only link. The new space is empty and doesn't match the earlier archive photos, so the jump is abrupt.

Cut from the 1954 demonstration room (grey, checkered floor) to a 1966 office. The change of look is large and rests on the caption alone. The narration 'In 1966' lands on the first frame of the new room, which is fine.

A card showing the 'ALPAC conclusion' dissolves into the office while its text is still visible, and the card text overlaps the subtitle. The previous shot, a close-up of a document, doesn't connect to the 'results were thin' narration.

A split-screen wipe puts '1966 postediting' beside 'today: post-editing' while the narration says 'part of the job'. The wipe is busy, and the next shot is a wide, empty office that doesn't illustrate the narration.

Cut from the translation-editor monitor to an office with a video-call setup. The narration moves from 'tasks MT cannot replace' to 'that is translation, the written word', but the picture shows an interpreter's video-call booth, which is spoken language. The picture doesn't match the words.

The 'Nuremberg 1945 / today' split-screen shows the video-call interpreter while the narration says 'court interpreters must be certified'. The next frames have no subtitle for about 1.5 s, and the wide shot of the empty video-call room shows the question 'the next ten years?' with nothing to look at.

The narration 'to the video call. In 1954, the...' cuts to the street at dusk. The next idea is the 1954 forecast, which is shown with a street shot instead of the lab. The reader has to work out that the street is the film's lamplighter metaphor.
R16.2 to R16.4 show a wide, mostly static video-call room with almost no movement, while several lines of narration run over it.
The street at dusk runs for about 10 consecutive frames (R17.6 to R18.7), roughly 40 s. The lamplighter walks slowly and the picture barely changes while the closing narration is spoken.
R10.4 to R10.8 hold on the same document close-up and typewriter shots across the 'postediting' and 'more translators available than work' beats. The views change only slightly.
